chapter_title: Capstone Project: Building a Complete Embedded System
chapter_summary:
The capstone project is the culmination of everything you have learned in this course. You will design, build, and test a complete embedded system that integrates multiple hardware and software components. The recommended project is a **Smart Home Controller** that combines all the concepts from the course.

**Project Requirements:**
1. The system has two user buttons (input) and an RGB LED (output).
2. Button 1 toggles between three modes: Security, Lighting, and Climate.
3. In Security mode, Button 2 arms and disarms the system. When armed, the LED is red. When disarmed, the LED is green. If the system is armed and a simulated intrusion is detected (via another switch or a timer), the LED blinks red and a message is sent via UART.
4. In Lighting mode, Button 2 cycles through LED colors: red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, magenta, white.
5. In Climate mode, the LED brightness changes based on a simulated temperature reading (using a potentiometer or a timer-based simulation). The UART sends temperature readings every 2 seconds.
6. The system uses an FSM to manage the three modes and their sub-states.
7. The system uses interrupts for button presses (debounced in software) and uses the main loop for periodic tasks like UART output and sensor reading.

**Design Process:**
1. **Requirements:** Write a clear list of what the system must do.
2. **Architecture:** Draw a block diagram showing the hardware components (LaunchPad, switches, LED) and the software components (FSM, UART, interrupts).
3. **State Diagram:** Draw the FSM state diagram showing all modes, sub-states, and transitions.
4. **Implementation:** Write the C code, starting with initialization, then the FSM, then the ISRs, then the main loop.
5. **Testing:** Test each mode independently, then test all transitions between modes. Use the UART to log state changes and errors.
6. **Debugging:** If a mode does not work, use functional debugging (dump state variables to UART) and the SysTick timer to measure timing.
7. **Documentation:** Write a brief report describing the system, how it works, and any challenges you faced.

**Implementation Tips:**
- Use a global `systemState` variable for the FSM state.
- Use an enum for the modes: `typedef enum { SECURITY, LIGHTING, CLIMATE } SystemMode;`
- Use a `volatile` flag for button presses that is set in the ISR and read in the main loop.
- Use modular functions: `initHardware()`, `runFSM()`, `sendStatus()`, `readSensor()`.
- Keep ISRs short: set a flag and return. Do the heavy work in the main loop.

**Alternative Capstone Projects:**
- **Digital Piano:** Use the UART to receive key presses, generate tones using PWM (if available), and implement a simple sequencer.
- **Autonomous Robot:** Use two distance sensors and an FSM to navigate a simple course (steer left, steer right, go straight).
- **Handheld Video Game:** Implement a simple game (like Pong or Snake) using switches for input and LEDs or a simple display for output.

screens.title: Capstone Project: Smart Home Controller
screens.subtitle: Integrate GPIO, UART, FSMs, and interrupts into a single embedded system

narration.text: This capstone brings together the core skills you’ve learned: direct GPIO control, serial communication, finite state machines, and interrupt-driven inputs. You will design and build a Smart Home Controller that uses two buttons and an RGB LED to represent three modes: Security, Lighting, and Climate. In Security mode the second button arms and disarms the system and triggers an alert over the UART when an intrusion is simulated. In Lighting mode the second button cycles LED colors. In Climate mode LED brightness reflects a simulated temperature and the UART reports readings periodically. This project shows why modular design matters: small, testable functions and short interrupt handlers keep behavior predictable. We’ll follow a disciplined process—requirements, architecture, state diagram, implementation, testing, debugging, and documentation—so you can develop incrementally and verify each part. By the end, you’ll have a working system, UART logs for verification, and a short report describing design choices and test results. Ready to plan the steps and begin building?

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.subtitle: Four verified competencies for the capstone

narration.text: By completing this capstone you will learn to design a full embedded system from requirements through documentation. First, you will translate functional specifications into a clear list of requirements that guide hardware choices and software behavior. Second, you will integrate GPIO, UART, finite state machines, and interrupts into a cohesive implementation so each mechanism works together without cross-talk. Third, you will follow a structured development process—architecture, state diagram, implementation, testing, and debugging—so you can build incrementally and verify each step. Fourth, you will test, debug, and document your final system, using UART logs and a short report or demo video to prove correctness. Each objective maps to a milestone you can verify: a requirements checklist, a correct FSM, working ISRs and main loop, and a test report. These skills are the practical glue that turns small examples into a complete product, and they mirror industry expectations for embedded prototypes.

screens.title: A step-by-step design workflow
screens.subtitle: Requirements → Architecture → State diagram → Implementation → Test → Debug → Document

narration.text: Good embedded design starts with clear requirements. For this capstone, write a concise list that includes the inputs, outputs, timing, safety constraints, and logging expectations. That list prevents scope creep and informs hardware choices. Next produce an architecture block diagram that maps hardware components to software modules—LaunchPad, switches, RGB LED, FSM module, ISR handlers, and UART logger. The state diagram is the heart: draw explicit modes and sub-states, list events that cause transitions, and annotate outputs for each state. When you implement, start with initialization functions then the FSM and ISRs, keeping interrupts short by setting flags and letting the main loop do work. Test each piece independently: verify buttons and LED behavior, then UART messages, then FSM transitions. Use UART logs to confirm state changes and timings. Debug with simple strategies: dump state variables, add timestamps, and isolate failing modes. Finally, document behavior, known issues, and the test plan. A concrete example: first implement Button 1 to cycle modes and log each change to UART; prove mode switches before adding the secondary behaviors. A common mistake is building all features at once—incremental verification saves time and reduces integration errors. What will you implement and test first?

keyIdea.title: Incremental development
keyIdea.text: Build and verify the system in small steps: requirements, block diagram, FSM, modular code, then test each mode independently.

screens.title: Formalizing the system requirements
screens.subtitle: Precise inputs, outputs, modes, and timing constraints

narration.text: A clear requirements list is the single best defense against scope creep. For the Smart Home Controller the requirements are concrete: two user buttons and an RGB LED; Button 1 cycles three modes—Security, Lighting, Climate; Button 2 performs mode-specific actions such as arming/disarming or cycling LED colors; a simulated intrusion triggers a blinking red LED and a UART message in Security mode; Lighting mode cycles seven colors; Climate mode maps a simulated temperature to LED brightness and sends temperature readings every two seconds over UART. Also specify software constraints: use an FSM for mode management, use interrupts for button presses with software debounce, and keep ISRs short by setting volatile flags. State precise behavior like LED colors for armed and disarmed states and the frequency of blink or telemetry. A typical mistake is leaving timing vague—state exact reporting intervals and debounce windows so tests are unambiguous. This list guides architecture and testing and becomes the checklist for grading. Formalizing the system requirements means document inputs, outputs, modes, exact behavior per mode, timing, and software constraints to guide design and testing.. In practical terms, precise inputs, outputs, modes, and timing constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Project Requirements
Requirements (formal)
  • Two buttons (mode, action) and an RGB LED output.
  • Mode cycle: Security, Lighting, Climate.
  • Security: Button 2 arms/disarms. Armed LED=red, Disarmed LED=green. Intrusion blinks red and sends UART alert.
  • Lighting: Button 2 cycles colors: red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, magenta, white.
  • Climate: LED brightness tracks simulated temperature. UART sends readings every 2 seconds.
  • Use FSM for modes, interrupts for button presses (debounced), main loop for periodic tasks.
Acceptance criteria
Define testable pass/fail checks that map to the rubric. Example: pressing Button 2 in Lighting mode cycles through exactly seven colors in order. UART must show temperature every two seconds in Climate mode.
Timing specifics
Debounce interval: 10–50 ms recommended. Temperature telemetry interval: 2 seconds. Alarm blink frequency: choose a visible blink, and log the alert once over UART.
Common mistake
Vague timing and incomplete acceptance tests make verification hard. Be explicit in the requirements document.

screens.title: Block diagram: hardware and software components
screens.subtitle: Map pins to modules and show message flow for UART and ISR flags

narration.text: An architecture block diagram makes responsibilities explicit and helps split work across modules. For our capstone the hardware blocks are the LaunchPad MCU, two user switches, an optional intrusion switch or simulation input, an RGB LED with appropriate resistors, and a potentiometer or timer to simulate temperature. On the software side, define modules for initialization, the FSM, ISR handlers, UART logger, and sensor reading. The ISR handlers should only set volatile flags for button presses and return immediately. The main loop polls these flags, calls runFSM to process transitions, and performs periodic tasks like sendStatus for UART and readSensor for temperature. Draw arrows from interrupts to flags, from flags to the FSM input, and from the FSM to outputs like LED color changes and UART messages. This clear separation lets you test modules independently: confirm UART works before relying on it for debug output, and test LED control early. A common misconception is to write long ISRs that do formatting or heavy work—avoid that by moving logic to the main loop. How will you partition functions across files? screens.title: Designing the FSM for modes and sub-states
screens.subtitle: Explicit states, transitions, and outputs for Security, Lighting, and Climate

narration.text: The finite state machine organizes behavior and prevents ambiguous responses to inputs. For this project define three top-level states: SECURITY, LIGHTING, and CLIMATE. In Security state include sub-states like ARMED and DISARMED, and a transient ALARM state triggered by intrusion. In Lighting define a currentColor index that cycles across the seven required colors. In Climate the state includes a temperature sample and PWM duty for brightness. Each transition should be triggered by clear events: the mode button cycles top-level states; the action button triggers mode-specific behavior; a sensor event generates an alarm transition. Explicitly annotate outputs for each state: LED color and UART messages. A concrete example: when in SECURITY and action button arms the system, set LED red and log "armed" over UART. A common misconception is to encode too much behavior in transitions instead of states; prefer states that own outputs and have brief transition guards. Designing the FSM before coding lets you map states to enum values and write a simple switch statement that is easy to test and extend. Designing the FSM for modes and sub-states means list explicit states and transitions, annotate expected outputs, and use the fsm as the single source of truth for system behavior.. In practical terms, explicit states, transitions, and outputs for security, lighting, and climate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: State clarity
keyIdea.text: List explicit states and transitions, annotate expected outputs, and use the FSM as the single source of truth for system behavior.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › State Diagram
Top-level FSM
Define an enum for modes and keep the current mode in a global systemState variable.
SECURITY
Sub-states: ARMED, DISARMED, ALARM. Outputs: LED red/green/blink and UART alert when intrusion occurs.
LIGHTING
Maintain color index. Action button cycles colors; outputs are discrete LED colors.
CLIMATE
Read simulated temperature, set LED brightness, and send telemetry every 2 seconds over UART.
Concrete mapping
Use a typedef enum for modes and store a small struct for sub-state values like armed flag or color index. The runFSM function switches on the current mode and handles inputs and outputs there.
Key Takeaway

Make the FSM the single source of truth. Keep transitions simple and assign outputs to states rather than scattering output logic.

screens.title: Handling buttons safely with interrupts and debounce
screens.subtitle: Use volatile flags, short ISRs, and software debounce

narration.text: Responsive inputs need interrupts, but interrupts must be disciplined. For button presses use the MCU's GPIO interrupt to detect edges, but keep the ISR minimal: set a volatile flag and return. Declare the flag volatile so the compiler does not optimize reads away. Debounce in software rather than in the ISR; a typical approach is to set a flag in the ISR and in the main loop sample the button after a short delay or require several consecutive stable reads before accepting the press. This avoids long ISR delays and race conditions. For example, have the ISR set button1Flag and button2Flag. In the main loop, when a flag is seen, perform a debounce check—wait 10 to 50 milliseconds, read the pin, and only then accept the press. A common mistake is putting long processing or UART formatting inside the ISR; that can block other interrupts and complicate timing. Another pitfall is failing to clear interrupt flags in the peripheral, which causes repeated triggers. Keep ISRs short, document which registers you clear, and test edge cases like button hold or rapid presses. How will you detect and validate bounce behavior during testing?

keyIdea.title: ISR hygiene
keyIdea.text: ISRs should only set volatile flags and clear interrupt status; perform debounce and heavy work in the main loop to preserve responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Interrupts & ISRs
ISR best practices
Use interrupts to capture events but pass responsibility to the main loop.
  • Declare volatile flags set by ISRs and read in main loop.
  • Keep ISR code minimal: set flag, clear peripheral interrupt, return.
  • Debounce in software in the main loop (10–50 ms or counter method).
  • Document which registers the ISR clears to avoid repeated triggers.
Example pattern
ISR: set buttonFlag = 1; clear GPIO interrupt; return. Main loop: if buttonFlag, perform debounce check, then process and clear buttonFlag.
Common mistake
Doing UART prints in the ISR or long computations there blocks other interrupts and can cause missed events.

screens.title: Using UART to observe and debug system behavior
screens.subtitle: Log mode changes, alarms, and telemetry for verification

narration.text: UART is your essential verification tool. Use it to log mode switches, ARM/DISARM events, intrusion alerts, and periodic temperature readings from Climate mode. Keep messages concise and machine-friendly where helpful: a short label and a numeric value are easy to parse. For example send messages like: Mode: Lighting, Color: 3 or Temp: 23C. During debugging add state dumps when a mode fails so you can see the current state, color index, and flags. If you use printf-style formatting, perform it in the main loop or inside helper functions called from runFSM—not in ISRs. A concrete pattern from the course is to implement a sendStatus() function called every two seconds or triggered by state changes. Use UART to timestamp events for timing bugs. A common misconception is to rely solely on LEDs for verification—visuals are helpful but UART logs provide exact timing and values. When tests fail, the UART trace tells you whether a flag was set, a state transition occurred, or a sensor value was stale, making debugging far faster. Using UART to observe and debug system behavior means use concise uart messages for mode changes and telemetry to make debugging and grading objective and fast.. In practical terms, log mode changes, alarms, and telemetry for verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logging patterns
Choose short, structured messages that help trace timing and state.
Mode change example: "Mode: Security"
Alarm alert: "ALARM: intrusion detected"
Telemetry: "Temp: 24.2 C" sent every 2 seconds
Code snippet (visual)
// sendStatus() called from main loop
void sendStatus(void) {
    // format short, deterministic messages

}
Keep message formatting out of ISRs. Use UART logs to confirm state transitions and timing behavior during tests.

screens.title: Modular functions and practical coding tips
screens.subtitle: initHardware, runFSM, sendStatus, readSensor and ISR patterns

narration.text: Modularity keeps the codebase readable and testable. The course recommends functions named initHardware(), runFSM(), sendStatus(), and readSensor(). initHardware configures clocks, sets GPIO directions and digital enables, and initializes UART. runFSM implements the state machine using a switch on the systemState variable and calls helper functions to set outputs. ISRs must be short; set volatile flags there and return. sendStatus handles UART output and is called periodically from the main loop or on state change. readSensor returns a simulated temperature; for hardware use ADC or a potentiometer, for the lab you can simulate with a timer. Use an enum like typedef enum { SECURITY, LIGHTING, CLIMATE } SystemMode to represent modes. Keep global state minimal and prefer small structs. A concrete implementation tip: after enabling a GPIO clock wait for it to be ready before configuring registers. A common bug is forgetting to enable the port clock or the digital enable bit, which prevents pins from functioning. By splitting responsibilities into small functions you can unit test each part and swap implementations later if needed. Modular functions and practical coding tips means implement small, focused functions for init, fsm, uart, and sensors so each can be developed and tested independently.. In practical terms, inithardware, runfsm, sendstatus, readsensor and isr patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Recommended function list

  • runFSM() — evaluate flags and sensor data, set outputs
  • sendStatus() — format and send UART messages

Practical tips
Always enable the GPIO clock and wait for it before configuring pins. Use enums for state clarity. Keep globals small and document volatile flags set by ISRs. Debounce in main loop and avoid heavy work in ISRs.

typedef enum { SECURITY, LIGHTING, CLIMATE } SystemMode;
volatile uint8_t button1Flag = 0; // set in ISR

screens.title: Test strategy and debugging techniques
screens.subtitle: Mode-by-mode tests, use UART for state dumps, and timing checks

narration.text: Testing should be systematic and reproducible. Begin by testing hardware primitives: confirm both buttons generate interrupts and the RGB LED responds to simple outputs. Next test the UART by sending a simple status message and confirming reception on your PC terminal. Then validate the FSM: test mode cycling alone, then test each mode's action button behavior. For Security mode verify armed/disarmed behavior and simulate intrusion to confirm blinking and UART alert. For Lighting mode step through color cycles and ensure the sequence and wrap-around are correct. For Climate mode check that brightness maps correctly to a sensor reading and that temperature is sent every two seconds. Use UART logs to dump the current state, flags, color index, and last sensor reading when a test fails. Measure timing with SysTick or timestamps in logs to find delays or missed interrupts. Debugging tips include isolating failing subsystems, reproducing failures with deterministic inputs, and adding temporary diagnostic logs only while debugging. Record your tests and include UART samples in your report so graders can reproduce your verification. Test strategy and debugging techniques means test basic i/o, uart, and fsm in isolation, then compose tests for full system behavior and collect uart logs as evidence.. In practical terms, mode-by-mode tests, use uart for state dumps, and timing checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Testing & Debugging
Test checklist
  1. Hardware I/O verification: buttons generate interrupts; LED responds.
  2. UART sanity: send and receive basic messages.
  3. Mode cycling: confirm mode changes and LED color mapping.
  4. Mode-specific actions: arm/disarm, color cycle, temperature mapping.
  5. Integration: full scenario with intrusion and telemetry running.
Debugging techniques
  • Use UART state dumps to show systemState, flags, and sensor values.
  • Reproduce failures with deterministic inputs and capture logs.
  • Measure timing with SysTick timestamps to find missed deadlines.
  • Isolate failing modules and add temporary diagnostics while debugging.
Pro tip

Keep a test log describing each test step, expected outcome, observed output, and any corrective action. Include UART traces as attachments.

screens.title: What to remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from the capstone

narration.text: As you complete the capstone keep three core ideas front of mind. First, modular design and clear interfaces let you test parts in isolation and reduce integration time. Second, keep ISRs minimal: use volatile flags and do heavy processing in the main loop to preserve responsiveness and avoid missed interrupts. Third, use UART logs as objective evidence: concise messages let you verify timing, state transitions, and sensor values during grading and debugging. These three practices together turn a collection of toy examples into a reliable, verifiable embedded system. Apply them in your implementation and in your report to show clear engineering judgment. What to remember means modularity, short isrs with flags, and uart logging are the pillars of a verifiable embedded project.. In practical terms, three compact reminders from the capstone. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Before you submit, run a quick checklist: 1) Does your system meet the functional requirements for all three modes, including correct LED behavior and UART messages? 2) Is your FSM implemented with a clear enum and transitions, and do your ISRs only set volatile flags? 3) Do you have test evidence—UART traces, a short report or demo video, and a state diagram? These items form the core of the grading rubric and will guide your final polish. If any item is missing, prioritize adding concise logs or a short note in your documentation describing the intent and any trade-offs. A small, well-documented system beats a large but unreliable demo. What to remember (Checklist) means functionality proof, fsm clarity, short isrs, uart logs, and documentation together form a complete, gradeable deliverable.. In practical terms, three compact concept cards to guide your final submission. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Submission Checklist
Functionality
All modes behave as required and transitions are reliable under button presses.
Evidence
Attach UART logs, screenshots, or a short demo video showing the modes and an intrusion event.
Documentation
Include requirement list, block diagram, state diagram, and a brief note on debugging and known issues.
Final Tip
A concise demo that is fully repeatable and well-documented earns higher marks than an over-ambitious but flaky system.

ai_generation_note:
Create a 15-minute capstone project walkthrough video. Show the project requirements, the state diagram being drawn, the code being written in the IDE, and the final system running on the LaunchPad. Use a split screen to show the hardware and the UART output simultaneously. Include a time-lapse of the breadboard wiring. End with a checklist of deliverables and a grading rubric.
